note: D6's security design attaches every mechanism to one already built rather than inventing any: a THIRD ceiling cascade over the same _consume(), an explicit purpose on the existing issue()/verify(), a pg_constraint query through the existing restricted_session fixture. Three facts were read out of the built code BEFORE designing and each changed the design rather than confirming it: scope_kind is String(16) so the natural deletion_ prefix does not fit (computed, not eyeballed); verify() orders by issued_at DESC LIMIT 1 with no purpose predicate, which is both the vulnerability and the reason a naive filter creates a SHADOWING bug; and _signup_scopes has no global scope for a stated reason that does NOT transfer to deletion, so patterning off it would reopen NFR14.102. Section 5a treats the GENERATED PRIVACY POLICY as a security artifact rather than documentation, because a false statement in it is a compliance failure: NFR14.101 is the subtle one, since NFR14.89 asserts a disclosure is present and nothing asserts it is true. Eight rows (DESIGN-1 to DESIGN-8) have no upstream requirement and are design findings recorded as obligations rather than notes; DESIGN-4 supplies the design REASON section 3 reads pg_constraint rather than ORM metadata, which had previously been stated only as a preference. Status counts, derived from the rows: 35 OK, 12 N/A, 1 Deferred, zero GAP. The single Deferred row is NFR14.90, the one partly-automated obligation; every SECURITY obligation is automated, which is a property of the subject (deletion, ceilings and constraints are all questions about state) rather than of effort.

construction/releasing-safely/nfr-design/security-design.md section 3 - carried forward from the functional design: two of the three 0007 columns are NOT NULL, so a flip of ondelete alone FAILS at migration time. A failing migration is the good outcome; the hazard is the reverse ordering (nullable first, ondelete flip deferred), which leaves the cascade live while the schema looks prepared. Section 3's test catches it because it asserts confdeltype, not nullability

construction/releasing-safely/nfr-design/security-design.md section 3 - the constraint NAMES in the database differ from the model's implied names on two constraints, demonstrably, because 0002 renamed a column with alter_column which does not rename its constraint. This is the DESIGN REASON section 3 reads pg_constraint rather than ORM metadata: a metadata-sourced assertion would assert against the document rather than the database. The failure mode is a vacuous pass - a migration written against implied names fails on a migrated database and PASSES against a metadata-created one, so a metadata-building suite stays green while production cannot migrate

construction/releasing-safely/nfr-design/security-design.md section 3 - FOUR pinned revision literals, not one (corrected 2026-10-25 after review found the first version named only test_no_d5_migration.py). tests/db/test_no_d5_migration.py:29 (EXPECTED_HEAD plus the revision COUNT), tests/db/test_migration_from_head.py:142, tests/db/test_migration_runs.py:121, and tests/auth/test_endpoints.py:194 - the last being body['migration_revision'], which is NOT a migration test: team.md's Deployment practice makes the health endpoint's applied revision part of the post-deploy SMOKE set, so a stale literal means the smoke check asserts an old revision against a freshly migrated host. tests/db/test_migration_rollback_is_total.py:117 asserts '0001' and is correctly EXCLUDED - the failed-migration path, which 0007 does not move; naming the exception matters as much as naming the list, because a blanket replace of the literal would be right and a blanket replace of 'the revision literal' would not. The pin moves as part of 0007's own change: updating a pin with intent and weakening a gate under pressure produce the same diff, and naming only one test made this look like a one-line update, so the other three would have surfaced as confusing CI failures mid-build - exactly the pressure under which a constant gets edited to make a test pass

construction/releasing-safely/nfr-design/security-design.md section 2 - ip_prefix_of verified by reading app/api/auth.py:74 rather than taken on trust. Two properties weaken the per-IP bound for this attack: a /24 prefix (deliberate, so one mobile NAT is not a per-user counter) means spanning prefixes never accumulates, AND an IPv6 address contains no dot so the WHOLE address becomes the scope value, giving each IPv6 caller its own counter. Neither is fixed here - narrowing re-introduces the per-user counter the built comment rejects, and changing the function touches three built routes in the last unit before release. The consequence recorded is that DEL_GLOBAL_DAILY is load-bearing and the per-IP scope is depth, the opposite of how a reader would rank them, so the sub-ceiling is not later traded away as redundant

construction/releasing-safely/nfr-design/security-design.md section 2 - the four new del_* counter rows fall under rate_limit_counter's EXISTING HOURS_48 retention (derived from DISPOSITIONS, not quoted), so no new retention entry is needed. Asserted rather than assumed because a new counter kind whose rows were never purged would accumulate one row per number per day indefinitely and nothing in the ceiling path would notice. The correctness property is that the purge window (48h) is LONGER than every ceiling window it serves (daily maximum), so a counter is never deleted while still being enforced against

construction/releasing-safely/nfr-design/security-design.md section 3 - MEASURED against a real PostgreSQL 16 on 2026-10-25, not reasoned about: pg_constraint is a system catalog and is NOT permission-filtered by table grant, where information_schema's views are. Two child tables with ON DELETE CASCADE, SELECT granted on one only, queried as a restricted role: information_schema saw the granted child only; pg_constraint saw BOTH. This matters because the governance suite records the exact near-miss - an ungranted table is invisible in information_schema so every gate silently stops covering it, and the money assertion skipped batch.default_fee until the grant was added, with the comment concluding a control that quietly narrows is worse than one that fails. Section 3 does NOT inherit that narrowing, and it is a property of the CATALOG CHOICE rather than of care: a future reader simplifying to information_schema.referential_constraints would reintroduce it silently and the test would keep passing
